In [[mathematics]], the '''plethystic exponential''' is a certain [[Operator (mathematics)|operator]] defined on (formal) [[power series]] which, like the usual [[exponential function]], translates addition into multiplication. This exponential operator appears naturally in the theory of [[symmetric function]]s, as a concise relation between the [[Generating function|generating series]] for [[Elementary symmetric polynomial|elementary]], [[Complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial|complete]] and [[Power sum symmetric polynomial|power sums]] homogeneous symmetric polynomials in many variables. Its name comes from the operation called [[plethysm]], defined in the context of so-called [[lambda ring]]s. 

In [[combinatorics]], the plethystic exponential is a [[generating function]] for many well studied sequences of [[Integer|integers]], [[Polynomial|polynomials]] or power series, such as the number of integer [[List of partition topics|partitions]]. It is also an important technique in the [[enumerative combinatorics]] of unlabelled [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graphs]], and many other combinatorial objects.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Pólya|first1=G.|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-1-4612-4664-0|title=Combinatorial Enumeration of Groups, Graphs, and Chemical Compounds|last2=Read|first2=R. C.|date=1987|publisher=Springer New York|isbn=978-1-4612-9105-3|location=New York, NY|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-4664-0}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Harary|first=Frank|date=1955-02-01|title=The number of linear, directed, rooted, and connected graphs|url=http://www.ams.org/jourcgi/jour-getitem?pii=S0002-9947-1955-0068198-2|journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society|language=en|volume=78|issue=2|pages=445–463|doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1955-0068198-2|issn=0002-9947|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

In [[geometry]] and [[topology]], the plethystic exponential of a certain geometric/topologic invariant of a space, determines the corresponding invariant of its symmetric products.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Macdonald|first1=I. G.|authorlink1=Ian G. Macdonald|date=1962|title=The Poincare Polynomial of a Symmetric Product|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0305004100040573/type/journal_article|journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]]|language=en|volume=58|issue=4|pages=563–568|doi=10.1017/S0305004100040573|bibcode=1962PCPS...58..563M |s2cid=121316624 |issn=0305-0041|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

The inverse operator of the plethystic exponential is the plethystic logarithm.

== Definition, main properties and basic examples==

Let <math>R[[x]]</math> be a ring of formal power series in the variable <math>x</math>, with coefficients in a commutative ring <math>R</math>. Denote by 

:<math>R^0[[x]] \subset R[[x]]</math> 

the ideal consisting of power series without constant term. Then, given <math>f(x)\in R^0[[x]]</math>, its plethystic exponential <math>\operatorname{PE}[f]</math> is given by

:<math>\operatorname{PE}[f](x)= \exp \left( \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{f(x^k)}k \right)</math> 

where <math>\exp(\cdot)</math> is the usual exponential function. It is readily verified that (writing simply <math>\operatorname{PE}[f]</math> when the variable is understood):

:<math>\begin{align}[ll]
\operatorname{PE}[0] & = 1\\[5pt]
\operatorname{PE}[f+g] & = \operatorname{PE}[f] \operatorname{PE}[g]\\[5pt]
\operatorname{PE}[-f] & = \operatorname{PE}[f]^{-1}
\end{align}</math>

Some basic examples are:
:<math>\begin{align}[ll]
\operatorname{PE}[x^n] & = \frac1{1-x^n}, n \in \mathbb{N} \\[5pt]
\operatorname{PE}\left[ \frac x{1-x} \right] & =  1+\sum_{n\geq1}p(n)x^n
\end{align}</math>

In this last example, <math>p(n)</math> is number of partitions of <math>n\in\mathbb{N}</math>.

The plethystic exponential can be also defined for power series rings in many variables.

==Product-sum formula==

The plethystic exponential can be used to provide innumerous product-sum identities. This is a consequence of a product formula for plethystic exponentials themselves. If <math>f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k x^k</math>  denotes a formal power series with real coefficients <math>a_k</math>, then it is not difficult to show that:<math display="block">\operatorname{PE}[f](x)=\prod_{k=1}^\infty (1-x^k)^{-a_k} </math>The analogous product expression also holds in the many variables case. One particularly interesting case is its relation to [[integer partition]]s and to the [[cycle index]] of the [[symmetric group]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Florentino|first=Carlos|date=2021-10-07|title=Plethystic Exponential Calculus and Characteristic Polynomials of Permutations|url=https://www.dmlett.com/archive/v8/DML22_v8_pp22-29..pdf|journal=Discrete Mathematics Letters|language=en|volume=8|pages=22–29|doi=10.47443/dml.2021.094|arxiv=2105.13049|s2cid=237451072 |issn=2664-2557}}</ref>

==Relation with symmetric functions==

Working with variables <math>x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n</math>, denote by <math>h_k</math> the [[complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial]], that is the sum of all [[monomial]]s of degree&nbsp;''k'' in the variables <math>x_i</math>, and by  <math>e_k</math> the [[Elementary symmetric polynomial|elementary symmetric polynomials]]. Then, the <math>h_k</math> and the <math>e_k</math> are related to the power sum polynomials: <math>p_k=x_1^k + \cdots + x_n^k</math> by [[Newton's identities]], that can succinctly be written, using plethystic exponentials, as:

:<math> \sum_{n=0}^\infty h_n \,t^n = \operatorname{PE}[p_1 \,t] = \operatorname{PE}[x_1 t + \cdots + x_n t] </math>
:<math> \sum_{n=0}^\infty (-1)^n e_n \,t^n = \operatorname{PE}[- p_1 \,t] = \operatorname{PE}[-x_1 t - \cdots - x_n t] </math>

== Macdonald's formula for symmetric products ==
Let ''X'' be a finite [[CW complex]], of dimension ''d'', with [[Poincaré polynomial]]<math display="block">P_X (t) = \sum_{k=0}^d b_k(X) \, t^k</math>where <math>b_k(X)</math> is its ''k''th [[Betti number]]. Then the Poincaré polynomial of the ''n''th symmetric product of ''X'', denoted <math>\operatorname{Sym}^n (X)</math>, is obtained from the series expansion:<math display="block">\operatorname{PE}[P_X(-t)\,x] = \prod_{k=0}^d (1-t^k x)^{(-1)^{k+1}b_k(X)} = \sum_{n\geq 0} P_{\operatorname{Sym}^n(X)}(-t) \, x^n </math>

==Plethystic logarithm==
The inverse of the plethystic exponential is the plethystic logarithm.  It is defined in the multivariate case as follows: if <math>f(x_1, \ldots, x_n)</math> is a formal power series{{efn|Or a function of {{mvar|n}} complex arguments.}} with constant term 1, then the plethystic logarithm <math>\operatorname{PL}[f]</math> is defined by
<math display="block">\operatorname{PL}[f](t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{\mu(k)}{k} \ln(f(t_1^k, t_2^k, \ldots, t_n^k)),</math>
where <math>\mu(k)</math> is the [[Möbius function]], defined by<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Abramowitz |first1=Milton |title=Handbook of mathematical functions: with formulas, graphs and mathematical tables [conference under the auspices of the National science foundation and the Massachusetts institute of technology] |last2=Stegun |first2=Irene A. |date=1972 |publisher=Dover |isbn=978-0-486-61272-0 |series=Dover books on advanced mathematics |location=New York |orig-year=1964|page = 826}}</ref>
<math display="block">\mu(k) = 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } k = 1, \\
(-1)^n & \text{if } k \text{ is the product of } n \text{ distinct primes}, \\
0 & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}</math>
and {{math|ln}} is the [[natural logarithm]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Benvenuiti |first1=Sergio |last2=Feng |first2=Bo | last3=Hanany | first3=Amihay | last4=He | first4=Yang-Hui |year=2006 |title=Counting BPS Operators in Gauge Theories |page=31 |arxiv= hep-th/0608050v2|quote= |mode= |journal= Journal of High Energy Physics|doi=10.1088/1126-6708/2007/11/050 }}</ref>

==The plethystic programme in  physics==
In a series of articles, a group of theoretical physicists, including Bo Feng, Amihay Hanany and [[Yang-Hui He]], proposed a programme for systematically counting single and multi-trace gauge invariant operators of [[Supersymmetric gauge theory|supersymmetric gauge theories]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Feng|first1=Bo|last2=Hanany|first2=Amihay|last3=He|first3=Yang-Hui|date=2007-03-20|title=Counting gauge invariants: the plethystic program|url=http://stacks.iop.org/1126-6708/2007/i=03/a=090?key=crossref.bcaed087696ada7ddb3caa309da4f9f7|journal=Journal of High Energy Physics|volume=2007|issue=3|pages=090|doi=10.1088/1126-6708/2007/03/090|arxiv=hep-th/0701063 |bibcode=2007JHEP...03..090F |s2cid=1908174 |issn=1029-8479}}</ref> In the case of quiver gauge theories of [[D-brane|D-branes]] probing [[Calabi–Yau]] singularities, this count is codified in the plethystic exponential of the [[Hilbert series]] of the singularity.
